Apple beats on quarterly revenue in CEO John Ternus’ first earnings report

Apple reported better-than-expected revenue but came up short of estimates on iPad sales for the fiscal fourth quarter.
Here’s how the company did compared to analysts’ estimates, according to LSEG.
EPS: $2.10.
Revenue: $114.48 billion vs. $113.39 billion expected
It’s Apple’s first earnings report since CEO John Ternus took the helm on Sept. 1, succeeding Tim Cook. CNBC isn’t immediately comparing the earnings figure to LSEG’s estimate of $1.99 per share.
Revenue increased 12% from $102.5 billion a year earlier, Apple said in a statement on Monday. The company reported iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion, topping estimates of $56.54 billion, according to LSEG.
Apple’s iPhone revenue in the quarter only included eight days of new Phone 18 Pro sales. And Apple’s new flagship device, the iPhone Duo, didn’t hit store shelves until the period was over.
During the quarter, Apple raised prices on iPhones by $100, reflecting a worldwide shortage on memory and other components.
Monday’s earnings call, set to start at 5 p.m. ET, will be the first with Ternus at the helm. Investors want to hear from him about the company’s plans in China after its AI software got approved, as well as the slew of recent product launches and how the company continues to grapple with global shortages of memory and flash storage.
Apple’s iPad division contracted over 10% on an annual basis during the quarter to $6.22 billion in sales. It was the worst performing of all of Apple’s product categories by growth.
The company released a new iPad Mini last month, and updated the iPad Air back in March, but the product line has not had many significant updates this year. Apple’s iPad division declined 6% year-over-year during the June quarter, too.
Ternus blamed supply constraints and a difficult comparison to last year as reasons for the iPad’s performance.
Gross margin in focus due to high component prices:
Apple’s gross margin is being closely watched as the company is being battered by higher prices for key components, such as storage, memory, and chips.
The gross margin was 47.9%, including a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point from tariff refunds. It’s a major drop from last quarter’s 50.1% gross margin.
It’s unclear if analysts factored any potential tariff refund impact in their projections. Had they not, gross margin would have been short of the 47.5% consensus estimate from LSEG.

Marvell to buy Lumentum in all-stock deal, a massive bet on AI connectivity

Marvell Technology on Monday said it will buy optical components maker Lumentum to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.
Since the tie-up is a fixed ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell’s takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn’t the company’s first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum’s stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.

text:
SpaceX at $1.8 trillion: is the real investment case rockets, Starlink or AI compute?

SpaceX at $1.8 trillion: is the real investment case rockets, Starlink or AI compute?
I've been looking through SpaceX's third-quarter results, and one thing strikes me: many discussions still treat it primarily as a space-launch business. The actual financial mix has changed remarkably fast. In Q3 2026, the Space segment produced $1.77 billion in revenue, Connectivity (mostly Starlink) $5.25 billion, and Super Intelligence $7.56 billion. The last category now includes data-center capacity, models and software, and the recently acquired Cursor.
That changes the way I would evaluate the company. The case for SpaceX used to rest heavily on its ability to launch cheaper than competitors, then turn that launch advantage into a satellite broadband business. This part is becoming demonstrably real. Starlink had 13.6 million consumer subscribers at September's end, with Connectivity producing $2.37 billion in quarterly operating income. You can argue about the long-term margin, but this is not some revenue-less space venture.
The catch is that consumer ARPU has fallen from $83 to $69 over the past year. Expansion into lower-income markets means the number of subscribers is not the whole story. And Starlink faces competitors, regulators and limits imposed by physics. A great product isn't guaranteed an unlimited customer base at American pricing.
Meanwhile, AI makes the valuation much harder. SpaceX had 1.7 GW of nameplate computing capacity at quarter end, and SI revenue is growing extraordinarily quickly as new cloud agreements become active. The thesis is that intelligence demand may rise faster than the supply of energized data-center capacity, allowing the owners of ready-to-run compute to earn scarcity rents. SpaceX can also consume that compute in Grok or its applications rather than selling all of it to third parties. That flexibility has value.
But look at the cash flow statement: $48.1 billion spent buying property and equipment in the first nine months versus $13.1 billion in operating cash flow. That leaves roughly negative $35 billion on a simple operating-cash-minus-capex basis. Management also expects $35–40 billion in capex in Q4 and has announced a proposed $40 billion GPU financing lease. A lot of today's earnings could end up supporting asset replacement rather than shareholder distributions if AI compute pricing falls or chip replacement cycles remain short.
Orbital compute is the genuinely fascinating wildcard. SpaceX's published Starmind design talks about 175 kW of average compute per satellite. To reach one gigawatt you would need roughly 5,700 such satellites, even before accounting for real-world losses. That shows why radically cheaper, frequent Starship launches might matter beyond broadband. It also makes the engineering problems hard to ignore: thermal radiation, hardware reliability, servicing, launch costs and orbital congestion are all nontrivial. I don't think it belongs in a central valuation yet.
At roughly $1.83 trillion in market cap as of October 30, this is not remotely a cheap conventional investment. My rough five-year range is $0.9 trillion in a bear case, $4.2 trillion in a base case, and $9 trillion in a bull case, with share dilution reducing the return from those market-cap outcomes. The result is attractive only if you give meaningful probability to AI and connectivity becoming enormous profit pools, not simply large revenue lines.
I'm curious how others would underwrite this. Would you value SpaceX chiefly as a launch-enabled communications utility, as an AI infrastructure business, or as an entirely new industrial platform? And which single metric would make you change your mind fastest: Starlink ARPU, compute cash returns, or Starship reuse?

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman Thinks It's 'Terrible' for You to Have RAM in Your PC

https://www.ign.com/articles/openai-ceo-sam-altman-thinks-its-terrible-for-you-to-have-ram-in-your-gaming-pc
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman thinks it's "terrible" for people to have RAM in their computers rather than in a data center, as the scarcity of memory caused by the AI boom continues to drive up costs. In an interview with YouTuber Cheeky Pint, Altman talked about the global compute supply problems facing the AI industry right now. And, when the conversation inevitably moved on to memory, Altman claimed that the "invisible hand" (of the market) is failing, likely because every DRAM wafer isn't flowing straight into a data center to run these AI models.
Altman said: "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer, and being used maybe 5% of the time. Like, you want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."
It kind of makes sense from Altman's perspective. It's in OpenAI's best interest to get as many hyperscaler data centers online to make its huge AI models as fast as possible. But, while Altman seems to believe that everyone is buying memory just to run local AI models, RAM is needed for nearly every kind of consumer electronics product, which is why every piece of gaming hardware has risen in price this year. Just this month, used PS5 Pros skyrocketed in price to $1,399, after the console got an official price increase in March due to the RAM shortage. Meanwhile, the RTX 5080 just disappeared off of Nvidia's marketplace, weeks after the RTX 5090 was all but discontinued.

It’s crazy watching how fast sentiment flipped on GOOGL right after earnings. People are suddenly bringing out all these bear cases while the actual business is as bullish as ever.
What makes this dip even wilder is comparing Alphabet to private AI valuations right now. Anthropic just filed for their IPO and they are eyeing a $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation. For $1.5T with Anthropic, you get $16.3B in first-half 2026 revenue, massive cash burn, no real consumer ecosystem, and hundreds of billions in future cloud compute bills because they don't own their own hardware.
Meanwhile, all of Alphabet is sitting around a $3.5T market cap. If the market really thinks a standalone LLM company renting compute is worth $1.5T, Wall Street is basically saying the rest of Google (Search, YouTube, Android, Google Cloud, Waymo, their investment portfolio, and the largest custom TPU fleet on earth) is only worth ~$2T combined. On top of that, people forget Google already owns a huge stake in Anthropic from backing them early, which is worth around 14% of ANT itself.
Just look at the actual growth numbers Alphabet put up in Q3 and how they positioned themselves for AI over the last decade. Revenue grew 25% YoY to $127.6B, putting Google on a half-trillion-dollar annual run rate, and operating income jumped 30% to $40.6B with a 31.8% operating margin. Everybody else spent the last three years scrambling to buy Nvidia GPUs at peak prices. Google spent the last ten years building custom TPUs, merging DeepMind and Google Brain, and plugging AI straight into products that billions of people already use every day across Android, Chrome, Workspace, Search, and YouTube.
Owning that whole stack is why Google Cloud is taking off right now. Cloud grew 103% YoY to $30.7B in a single quarter, pulling in $11.1B in operating income (~36% margin) with a massive $561B backlog. People who still think Google is just an ad play need to understand TPUs and how they changed GCP. When AI labs like Anthropic and enterprise customers spend tens of billions on compute, a huge chunk of that money goes right into Google Cloud. Cloud is legitimately on track to catch or pass Search by 2030.
The biggest bear argument I keep seeing in the comments is always "how many ads can an AI chatbot really get people to click on?"
If you think AI monetization is about blue links and click volume, you're getting it wrong. It is not going to be about the clicks at all. Ads and shopping will integrate directly into the dynamic user based response, and if they execute that right, that alone has more revenue potential than the entire legacy Search business.
With traditional Search, you typed a 3-word keyword, Google gave you 10 links, and advertisers paid hoping you might click one and eventually buy something. The intent was scattered and Google only got a tiny slice of the transaction.
Conversational AI changes that completely. Instead of just dumping links on you, the AI actually guides the buying decision. You ask Gemini a question and it tells you, "Hey I found this option at X price, but I also found this one at Y price, and let me tell you why the second one is better for your setup and why you should pick it."
When you pair that kind of direct recommendation with the insane amount of data Google already has across Search, YouTube, Gmail, Chrome, and Maps, the upside is basically unlimited. Advertisers won't just be bidding on blind clicks anymore, they'll be paying for actual conversions right inside the chat. Google hasn't turned this on yet and I don't think they will rush it in the near future while they lock in the user base, but let’s say in a year or two we will see native AI monetization print money way faster than traditional search ads ever did.
Even outside of AI and Cloud, the core business is still a monster. Search grew to $63.3B for the quarter, YouTube ads pulled in $11.2B alongside strong subscription growth, and Waymo is quietly scaling real autonomous commercial rides across major cities while competitors are still showing off concepts. Some people talk about Google right now like it's a heavily indebted company struggling to survive because of the $51.4B capex number, completely ignoring that Alphabet has massive cash flow and the balance sheet to fund its data center buildout themselves.
I cannot think of a company better positioned to take advantage of AI and the future of internet services than Google. I truly believe Google will be a $10T company within a decade.

REDDIT - My bear, base and bull analysis

Disclaimer : I redacted my post partially with AI as English isn't my main language. I own every argument stated in this post and used my own way of calculating the future share prices. Please feel free to criticize my method.
This post is a follow up to my yesterday's analysis on NOW : https://www.reddit.com/r/ValueInvesting/comments/1xit19a/now_down_25_after_q3_my_thesis_with_full_numbers/
I adjusted my method to take into account the relevant commentaries and reproduce the exercice on REDDIT which I also own
-------------
Q3 results :
Revenue: $895M, +53% - Beat
Profitability:
net income $283M (32% margin)
free cash flow $363M (40% of revenue).
Users:
global DAUq 130.3M (+12%), but US DAUq 50.7M (down from 53.2M in Q2).
Logged-in DAUq grew 7%
Monetization:
US ARPU was $13.82, +53%
Logged-in and app users drive more than 80% of monetization.
Q4 guide:
revenue $1.00–1.03B (+38–42%), EBITDA margin ~49%.
If Google search referrals keep falling (AI Overviews), total DAUq could drop by a low double-digit percentage.
Balance sheet:
$3.0B of cash and no debt.
Reddit bought back $100M of stock in Q3, with ~$660M left on the authorization.
Moat and risks
The moat:
20 years of human, topic-organized conversation that nobody can easily recreate. This is why LLMs want to license the data and why advertisers now pay +53% per US user. The engaged core (logged-in, app) is still growing.
The risk:
A large part of logged-out traffic came from Google, and AI answers now intercept it. Data licensing renewals, including Google’s, are not signed yet.
Reddit is a "niche" product for some people, not growing as fast as META's apps
The three scenarios (skip to the table below if you don't feel like reading the details)
Bear: Google cuts the pipe, and the logged-in wall shrinks the audience
Search referrals keep collapsing, US DAUq falls for several quarters, and the logged-in wall cuts the remaining logged-out reach.
Ad growth slows to +14% in 2027, then +7% and +5%. That is the Q4 DAUq warning playing out in full, partly offset by ARPU.
Data licensing deals are not renewed. Net margin is stuck at 25%, below today’s 32%, because costs stay while growth disappears.
SBC climbs to 15% of revenue (retention grants after the crash), so the share count keeps rising despite buybacks.
Priced like a no-growth ad platform: ~14× earnings.
EPS in 2029 roughly equals 2026’s: three lost years.
Base: fewer visitors, better monetized
Total DAUq dips in Q4 and stabilizes, international keeps growing, and the logged-in core keeps growing mid-single digits.
ARPU carries growth: more advertisers (Reddit Max adoption ×3 QoQ), better targeting on logged-in users, and lower-funnel ads
Revenue grows +27% in 2027, below the ~32% consensus set before Q3, then naturally slows down +21% Y+2 and +17% Y+3.
Net margin goes from 32% to 35% as SBC falls from ~13% to 11% of revenue as it grows.
Exit at ~23× earnings, for a business still growing mid-teens after 2029.
Bull: the logged-in bet works
Logged-in conversion offsets the lost search traffic, international monetization starts closing results
Revenue grows +36% / +28% / +22%, reaching ~$7.2B in 2029, above management’s next $5B milestone.
Net margin reaches 38%, SBC falls to 9% of revenue, and buybacks almost offset dilution.
Exit P/E ~28×, deliberately below where high-growth ad platforms have traded. No narrative premium.
SBC and buybacks: SBC runs at ~15% of revenue today ($131M in Q3). In my numbers it keeps growing ~14–15% a year in every scenario, slower than revenue except in the Bear. The $1B buyback program only offsets part of the dilution: I assume the share count still rises in all three scenarios, even in the Bull. That’s deliberately conservative, since diluted shares were slightly down YoY.
Exit multiples: I start from historical ranges (16× / 24× / 28× earnings). I then adjust them for where the US 10-year might be in 2029: 5.75% / 5.0% / 4.25% vs a 4.4% reference. At ~$95, the market currently pays ~9.4× my 2029 Base EPS
Scenario Revenue growth Y+1 / Y+2 / Y+3 Net margin Y+3 (GAAP, after SBC) SBC CAGR (3 yrs) Net share count CAGR (3 yrs)* Diluted shares (Y+3) EPS Y+3 (GAAP, after SBC) Exit P/E (rate-adjusted) Share price (Y+3) Bear +14% / +7% / +5% 25% +14.1% +1.8% 213M $5.08 13.8× $70 Base +27% / +21% / +17% 35% +15.2% +1.3% 210M $10.12 22.6× $228 Bull +36% / +28% / +22% 38% +13.9% +0.7% 206M $13.23 28.4× $376
Weighted 25/50/25, the target is ~$226 by late 2029: +138% from $95, or 33% a year.
Why GAAP net income and not FCF − SBC? With almost no capex, GAAP net income already deducts SBC and is the cleaner earnings figure in my opinion. FCF − SBC was 26% of revenue in Q3, below the 32% net margin. The gap comes from working capital (receivables growing with +53% revenue) and interest income. Over time the two should converge.
I wont add my own opinion of the probability of each scenario as I try to stay numbers focused. Just note that I try to make Bear a complete Bear with all going wrong, and Bull all going right.

* I do take into account SBC in my way of calculation ;
* I used what I believe are conservative ratios, taking into account the current fed rates as well as "non narrative driven" multiples. This is a value sub.
* I don't care if you don't like reddit and I don't care if you love it. I'm only talking with numbers and try to embrace everyone's opinion with a Bear, Base and Bull scenario
* I am not a wanna be analyst, a bag holder or a permabull/bear ; I'm just someone trying to improve and genuinly interested in the market, trying to find value to have a better life down the road, which I also wish to you all.

text:
Reddit is Paying the Price for Independence. Execution will be key.

I think that the market is repricing Reddit to account for the potential low double-digit decline in DAUq, recognizing that the loss of search traffic combined with the friction of requiring users to log in could have a meaningful impact on future growth and monetization. And some of that concern is justified. There will likely be pain during this transition, and success is certainly not guaranteed.
But I also think Steve got ahead of this and was unusually upfront about the problem and the proposed solution. Rather than slowly watching Reddit become increasingly dependent on a search ecosystem that is changing rapidly, management appears to be ripping the band-aid off and moving toward a more controlled, authenticated platform.
The vision is a Reddit that is less dependent on Google's referrals, has a more direct relationship with its users, better understands its audience, and can improve personalization, retention, advertising targeting, and ultimately monetization.
The transition could initially mean slower user growth, or even declining DAU. But total users and revenue aren't necessarily interchangeable. If Reddit can retain and better monetize its logged-in audience, it doesn't necessarily need to recover every last logged-out visitor it loses.
The market is likely pricing in a fairly pessimistic version of Reddit's future and that leaves room for management to prove said market wrong. Of course, this is a major strategic transition, again, without a guarantee of success. The next few quarters will be important. Likely will need to keep watching logged-in engagement, retention, ARPU, and free cash flow. The near-term pain may be real, but so is the opportunity if this strategy works.

“AI is a bubble.” mmm NO.

​
Apparently everyone has suddenly become Warren Buffett after watching three YouTube videos and reading a bearish headline.
Lets get something straight.
Yes, there will be overvalued companies. Yes, some AI stocks will crash. Not every company with AI in its presentation deserves a billion dollar valuation.
But calling AI a bubble and dismissing the entire technological revolution? That's a different kind of stupidity.
J.P. Morgan estimates global AI capex could reach $900 billion in 2026. Big Tech isn't spending that kind of money because ChatGPT wrote them an inspirational quote.
We're building the infrastructure for a completely new technological era. AI is already transforming software, healthcare, finance, manufacturing and practically every industry.
Remember the people who thought the internet was just a fad? Some of them are probably still explaining why Amazon is overvalued.
Here is the reality: the dot com bubble didnt kill the internet. It separated the winners from the losers.
And thats exactly what will happen here.
You dont have to buy every AI stock. You don't even have to like AI.
But confidently declaring the end of a revolution that is barely getting started doesnt make you a genius investor. It might just make you the guy explaining 10 years from now why you never saw it coming.
This isnt the end of the AI story. Its the beginning. And most people are still too busy arguing about the bubble to understand whats actually being built.
P.S. Being bearish isnt a personality. And saying "I told you so" after every market correction isn't an investment strategy.
TL;DR: AI isnt a bubble just because you missed the opportunity. Some stocks will crash, but the technology is here to stay. The internet had a bubble too. Look how that turned out.

text:
Intel stock plunges 16% as chipmaker blames PC slowdown for weak guidance

Intel shares plummeted in extended trading on Thursday after the chipmaker issued a weak fourth-quarter forecast, citing continued softness in the global PC market.
Here’s how the company did in the third quarter, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
Earnings per share: 52 cents adjusted vs. 40 cents expected
Revenue: $16.51 billion vs. $16.5 billion expected
Revenue climbed 21% from $13.7 billion a year earlier, the company said in a press release.
However, revenue in Intel’s client computing and physical AI group fell 5% from the same quarter a year ago to $8.1 billion, missing estimates, even as data center and AI revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion.
Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research.
For the current quarter, Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG.
“We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year, but we remain optimistic about the opportunities across our broader portfolio,” said Intel finance chief David Zinsner, in the release. “We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth.”
Additionally, Intel’s forecast reflects the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. Zinsner told Reuters that the incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, and said the company plans to start ramping up production there by the end of the week.
Intel’s stock has been on an upward tear, up about 150% so far this year, although it’s down roughly 23% in October as concerns have emerged about the size of the artificial intelligence buildout.
Known best for its industry leading central processing units, or CPUs, Intel has been a beneficiary of the rise in agentic AI. While chatbots and large models rely heavily on graphics processors from Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, agentic applications such as Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots lean on CPUs to help orchestrate tasks and data from a computer operating in the cloud.
“Despite near term headwinds affecting the broader PC industry, we continue to see robust demand for CPUs and more broadly, for all our computing platforms in the long term,” CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in the press release.
Nvidia, which has become the world’s most valuable company thanks to its dominance in GPUs, is scheduled to report results on mid-November. AMD reports next week.
Intel’s foundry business, meanwhile, has struggled to find its footing.
Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.
While Intel remains the only major customer of the chip, analysts say a major fabless chip customer could choose Intel with its next chip, 14A.
“People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC’s arm and keep them honest on pricing,” said TechInsights analyst Dan Hutcheson. “All the big ones have been testing there.”
On top of the memory shortages, another critical component of chipmaking known as substrates “are really constrained,” Intel’s Zinsner said in August.
The Trump administration took a 10% stake in the Intel last year after the company had fallen behind on its 7- and 10-nanometer technologies. Nvidia and Softbank also invested billions in Intel last year.
Tan has taken a more cautious approach to foundry spending than his predecessor, Pat Gelsinger, who launched an ambitious revival of the company’s foundry business.
Last week, Intel said crews have installed the first structural truss at its huge Ohio chip fab that was originally expected to deliver chips in 2025. Its next fab in Arizona is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028.
Oracle disclosed an expanded deal with Intel this week, announcing at its annual AI conference that it would deploy the chipmaker’s next-generation Xeon server processors, as well as the latest rack-scale systems from Nvidia and AMD, as it continues to add data center capacity.

Why Viasat Could Fit Amazon’s Space Ambitions
Farrar pointed to growing expectations of an Amazon-Viasat deal in his recent note, “Prepare for the Musk vs Bezos cage fight,” following the Satellite Innovation conference in California.

In his view, pairing Viasat’s spectrum and geostationary satellites with Amazon’s low Earth orbit network could boost its government and aviation business, while sharpening its challenge to SpaceX.
ASTS’ Rival Play Faces An Uphill Battle
AST SpaceMobile’s rival effort would face funding and management hurdles, according to Farrar. “I’m also told AST has attempted to put together a rival bid, but that would require significant support from the telcos, and would be vehemently opposed by Viasat management,” he said.

He also predicted an Amazon takeover would end Equatys, Viasat’s venture with Space42, as a satellite project. But Amazon would still need to work with Space42 to coordinate L-band spectrum access in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

text:
Insiders sell ~$20 for every $1 they buy. Here's how to tell which Form 4s actually matter (with two live examples)

Every quarter someone posts "insiders dumped $XXB!!" and the top reply is "nothing burger, it's stock comp." Both are partly right. Here's the 60-second filter I use on a Form 4 before I take it seriously.
1. Check the transaction code - S = open-market sale - P = open-market purchase - F = shares withheld to pay tax on vesting - M = option exercise
F and M are almost always noise. Most of the scary headline totals are S trades plus a pile of these.
2. Check the 10b5-1 box Since April 2023, Form 4 has a checkbox showing whether a trade was made under a pre-arranged trading plan. Planned sales were scheduled months earlier and carry little information.
3. Look for cluster buys after a drawdown Several insiders buying with their own cash after a big drop is the classic signal. Live example from last week, straight from EDGAR:
Rapport Therapeutics (RAPP), 21–23 Oct 2026: - 6 insiders bought: the CFO plus five directors - 7 open-market purchases, about $1.66M total - Prices between $26.10 and $27.36 - The largest was a director buying 35,714 shares (~$974K) - The CEO's only Form 4 that week was a small sale (2,210 shares, ~$64K), so "CEO buying" claims floating around are wrong
That's the pattern people look for: several board members writing checks at once after the stock fell hard. It still isn't a guarantee. Biotech insiders can be just as wrong about trial data as anyone else.
4. Read the footnotes A "P" can also be a purchase in an underwritten offering at the offering price. That reads very differently from someone hitting "buy" on the open market.
5. Size it against their holdings A $1M sale from someone holding $2B of stock is nothing. A $1M buy from a director whose entire stake was $3M is something.
Live sell-side example: Sea Limited (SE)
Five executives, including CEO Forrest Li and COO Ye Gang, sold about $25.06M between 25 and 28 Aug 2026, all under 10b5-1 plans. The stock then fell 31.3% ($108.68 on 14 Sep → $74.63 on 23 Oct). It looks damning in hindsight, but by this filter it's low signal: planned, small relative to their stakes, and nobody has changed course since.
Source: SEC EDGAR Form 4s. Not advice.
What filters do you use? Anyone actually backtested cluster buys vs. single-insider buys?

text:
Good Opportunity for Gold?

Now I know that gold is a classic rare metal that people should have some exposure to in their accounts anyway, but I think there is potential for a longer run over the coming years, so I am going to make my bull case and bear case. I already have a small position, but I am also planning on purchasing more at the current prices. My ETF of choice is GLD since it tracks the spot price directly and also has an annual expense ratio of 0.4%. If anyone prefers a different method, feel free to say as much in the comments. I have considered buying physical as well.
My Bull Case for buying @ ~$366
GLD sits about 28% below its 52-week high of $509.70. I realize the run up was a good selling opportunity, but gold is still hovering near $4,000 after a sharp pullback. I feel like investors typically fall into two camps after a big correction: this is either a good opportunity to buy in, or the rally is over. So why'd it drop so much? A combo of interest rate expectations, Treasury yield increases, and the dollar momentarily strengthening. I’ll touch on this more in the bear case.
Over the last 25 years, gold has outperformed the S&P by about double (938% vs 461%). I know 25 years is pretty arbitrary as far as time horizons go, but I am planning on holding for a long time.
The US federal debt keeps climbing and climbing. In fiscal year 2026 we hit a record $1.05 trillion in net interest payments. I repeat - over $1T on interest alone! How is the US government planning on reining this in? In my opinion, the likeliest path forward is policies that tolerate inflation and erode the true value of the debt. I foresee a lot of money printing in the near future. In this case, people holding cash lose out.
Have the structural reasons for buying gold changed in the last few years? Has the US eliminated its fiscal deficit? Has the debt begun shrinking? Has federal interest expense returned to historical norms? Have the central banks stopped diversifying reserves? Has the global monetary system suddenly become more disciplined? I am inclined to say no to all of these questions. The short-term circumstances for gold provide some pretty strong headwinds (see the bear case), but I think the long-term forces still apply.
Gold still matters from a de-dollarization perspective. No fiat currency has ever survived in the history of mankind, and the US dollar can go the same way. Gold can’t be printed like fiat, and there is continued instability in the Middle East. That cuts both ways, though - the conflict supports gold as a safe haven, but it has also strengthened the dollar and kept energy prices elevated (again see bear case).
As far as following the “smart” money goes, central banks bought over 1,000 metric tons a year from 2022 through 2024, and still added 863 tons in 2025.
A minor, but legitimate, player is the AI build out. Gold in electronics accounts for ~7% of annual gold demand, compared to jewelry, central bank buying, and investment demand. Figured I would include it since this is a global movement.
My Bear Case for avoiding @ ~$366
Gold pays no yield, and higher interest rates or other strong performing assets apply pressure or are at least tempting/more exciting.
A stronger dollar can pressure it, as we’ve seen recently, even if its momentary.
Reuters reported on Oct 12 that the dollar was near its strongest level in a year and a half, helped by safe-haven demand amid the war in Iran. Higher energy prices are likely to keep inflation elevated, and the SPR is at historic lows. Pressure on other routes to get oil out of the Middle East is exacerbating this.
All of this points to Warsh keeping interest rates high or pushing them higher. Keep in mind that we are expecting another Fed rate decision on Oct 28, and a hike is definitely on the table.
The 30 year Treasury bonds are at ~5.3%.
Some critics think the growth of the US economy could outpace the debt (I don’t personally agree with this).
Possible PT?
Just using this part to say that historical performance is not a guarantee of future price action. Gold can always stop climbing for a number of reasons, and just because gold’s historical rebounds from large corrections have seen it climb higher doesn’t mean that will happen again. Not financial advice, lol.
Quick math on a possible 5-year price target using gold’s 25-year return (938%):
The multiple of a 938% return = 938/100 + 1 = 10.38x
Annualized return over 25 years = 10.38^(1/25) - 1 = 1.098 - 1 = 0.098, or 9.8% a year
Applying that rate for 5 years = 1.098^5 = ~1.6x
Apply that multiple to the current price: $366 * 1.6 = ~$586. Shave off about 2% for fees and call it ~$575.
That’s about $65 above the 52-week high of $509.70, or roughly 57% above today’s price. That doesn't seem like much in this crazy bull market, but since it is the world reserve asset, I think it is a good play in this environment. I plan to DCA my position over the next few months. Can it can go lower? Yup, I just know I am not buying at the top! Thoughts?

text:
Reddit ($RDDT) Stock Thesis - $250 2027 Price Target

Disclosure
I am currently invested in Reddit (RDDT), and a large portion of my investment portfolio is allocated to the stock.
Introduction
I believe Reddit is a fast-growing company with expanding margins, increasing user growth, and significant long-term potential. I also believe the company has substantial upside potential from AI licensing deals that could materialize over the next year or so.
I believe Reddit is one of the most compelling investment opportunities in the market. I would like to use this post as an opportunity to surface other ideas, identify potential gaps in my thesis, and learn about any additional research or insights that other investors may have uncovered regarding Reddit stock.
Sections Covered
Reddit’s Unique Value Proposition
User Trends and Revenue Per User (RPU)
Reddit’s Advertising Evolution and Monetization Potential
Revenue Growth and Margin Expansion
Balance Sheet and Share Repurchases
AI Licensing Revenue
Company Valuation
Risks
Conclusion & Price Targets
Reddit’s Unique Value Proposition
Reddit is one of the last places on Earth with a vast array of human-generated content across different communities, subcategories, backgrounds, and demographics. One of its closest competitors is Facebook, but Reddit generally has much more human-written content, whereas other platforms like Facebook and Instagram are much more driven by photos and videos. Reddit is much more focused on text and actual writing.
I think this becomes increasingly valuable in a world of AI, where less and less content is written by humans. Reddit is one of the last places where that type of content remains prevalent.
Reddit is currently the third most-visited website in the world. In my own anecdotal experience, I have never written long posts on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, or any other social media platform, but I do write extensive content on Reddit, just as I am doing right now with this post. I think many other people and communities have a similar experience using the platform.
User Trends and Revenue Per User (RPU)
Reddit continues to demonstrate strong user growth across both daily active uniques (DAUq) and weekly active uniques (WAUq).
Daily active uniques increased from 110.4 million in Q2 2025 to 130.3 million in Q2 2026, representing 18% year-over-year growth.
Weekly active uniques increased from 416.4 million in Q2 2025 to 514.6 million in Q2 2026, representing 24% year-over-year growth.
International user growth across both daily and weekly active uniques is outpacing growth in the United States, which I believe is largely due to the U.S. market being more saturated. Nevertheless, both metrics are growing at healthy year-over-year rates, demonstrating Reddit's continued ability to expand its user base both domestically and internationally.
In addition to user growth, Reddit has significantly increased its revenue per user over the past year.
In Q2 2025, the average U.S. user generated $7.87 in revenue per quarter. By Q2 2026, that figure had increased to $11.85, representing more than 50% year-over-year growth.
International users generated an average of $1.73 per quarter in Q2 2025, compared with $2.26 in Q2 2026, representing more than 30% year-over-year growth.
As more people use Reddit, become invested in their communities, and spend more time on the platform, Reddit becomes increasingly valuable to advertisers. This creates an opportunity for revenue per user to continue increasing as the company improves its monetization.
The underlying cycle is straightforward: more users, better monetization, better recommendations, and higher conversions.
Evercore currently estimates that Meta generates approximately $100 per quarter in revenue per U.S. user. Based on Reddit's current U.S. revenue per user of $11.85 per quarter, Reddit generates only about one-eighth of what Meta generates from its U.S. users.
If Reddit can eventually reach even one-quarter, one-third, or one-half of Meta's current revenue per U.S. user, the company could have substantial additional upside from monetization alone. This potential exists alongside Reddit's continued user growth, with its user base expanding quarter after quarter and year after year.
Reddit’s Advertising Evolution and Monetization Potential
Reddit rolled out Reddit Max in September 2026 and recently made it generally available to all advertisers. Reddit is still relatively early in its monetization journey and has not yet reached the level of advertising performance and optimization that many competitors, including Google, Amazon, and Meta, have achieved.
Here are some of the biggest improvements Reddit Max has introduced for advertisers:
1. AI-Powered Campaign Automation
Reddit Max uses AI-powered campaign automation to help advertisers manage their campaigns more effectively. This includes automatically adjusting bids, budgets, audiences, and creative testing, reducing the need for advertisers to manage these settings manually.
2. Better Audience Targeting
Historically, Reddit has been somewhat weaker at targeting the correct audiences. However, its targeting capabilities are becoming more precise through scalable advertising audiences and AI-driven data analysis that can better match advertisements to Reddit's communities and subreddits.
3. Creative Optimization and Scalability
Previously, many advertising adjustments, including headline editing, image rotation, and video formatting, had to be completed manually by advertisers. This could result in underperforming advertisements remaining active without being identified or corrected.
Reddit's optimization engine can now automatically make many of these adjustments, helping advertisers improve creative performance and scale their campaigns more efficiently.
4. Better Performance Measurement and Transparency
Reddit is improving the metrics, key performance indicators (KPIs), research, and reporting available to advertisers across its platform. These improvements give advertisers better insights into purchasing decisions, leads, app activity, clicks, engagement, and attrition, helping them evaluate campaign performance more effectively.
5. Easier Adoption for Larger Advertisers and Agencies
Reddit's advertising API now integrates with Smartly, a third-party advertising management platform. This integration gives more advertisers and agencies access to Reddit's advertising ecosystem and provides additional resources for managing and scaling campaigns on the platform.
Overall, I believe these improvements are important because Reddit is still developing its advertising capabilities. As the platform improves its automation, targeting, creative optimization, measurement, and accessibility for larger advertisers, it has an opportunity to improve advertising performance and generate more revenue from its growing user base.
Revenue Growth and Margin Expansion
Reddit grew revenue by just over 60% year over year in its most recent quarter, Q2 2026. Revenue reached $805 million for the quarter, bringing total revenue over the last 12 months to $2.78 billion.
Profitability metrics also showed significant growth, with net income increasing 183%, free cash flow increasing 135%, and earnings per share (EPS) increasing 177% year over year.
Reddit generated $216 million in free cash flow in its most recent quarter and just over $1.02 billion in free cash flow over the last 12 months. These figures demonstrate the company's ability to translate its revenue growth into substantial cash generation.
Reddit's margins are also expanding. In Q2 2025, its gross margin was 90.81%, compared with 91.27% in Q2 2026. Operating margin increased from 13.55% to 28.79%, while profit margin increased from 17.87% to 31.41% over the same period.
In a nutshell, as Reddit reaches scale, it is becoming more profitable, not less.
For example, according to Reddit's annual 10-K filings, the company had 2,233 full-time employees at the end of 2024. By the end of 2025, that number had increased by 14.42% to 2,555 employees.
Reddit's revenue growth and profitability growth are clearly outpacing its employee growth. As the company reaches scale, it does not need to hire employees at nearly the same rate at which it can increase monetization and grow its user base.
I believe this operating leverage is an important part of the investment thesis. If Reddit can continue growing revenue substantially faster than its operating expenses, it has the potential to expand margins and increase profitability as the business scales.
Balance Sheet and Share Repurchases
In the most recent quarter, Reddit had $2.79 billion in cash on hand and zero debt. The company has no debt obligations weighing it down and is sitting on nearly $3 billion in cash, which represents more than 10% of its market capitalization as of October 27, 2026, the date I am writing this.
Additionally, Reddit announced a $1 billion share repurchase program this year. I believe the company could increase the size of this program over time as it becomes more profitable. If the shares remain cheap, Reddit could potentially expand the program within the next couple of quarters. This is my estimate and has not been confirmed by management.
AI Licensing Revenue
This is where we start to get into a bit of speculation. I want to clarify that I do not have access to the terms of these deals, and no one truly knows what they will be worth other than Reddit itself and the partners it is negotiating with, such as Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI.
However, the vast majority of analysts appear to have consistent expectations that AI licensing revenue will be significantly higher when these deals are renegotiated in the coming months and years.
Google announced its AI licensing deal with Reddit in February 2024, and OpenAI announced its licensing deal in March 2024. Anthropic does not currently have an AI licensing deal with Reddit and is involved in ongoing litigation with the company. A court ruling allowing Reddit's lawsuit to proceed has increased the possibility of a settlement. That said, none of this is guaranteed. These figures are estimates, and we will not know the final terms until the outcomes become clear in the coming months and years.
That said, I believe AI licensing revenue represents a significant opportunity for Reddit.
In the photo below, I will include a breakdown of Reddit's revenue by type. You will see advertising revenue and other revenue. The other revenue category includes Reddit's AI data licensing revenue. Over the last 12 months, Reddit has generated approximately $150 million in other revenue, which I believe primarily reflects its AI licensing revenue.
My personal belief is that when the Google and OpenAI deals are renegotiated in the coming months and years, their value could be significantly higher than $150 million per year combined. If other companies, including Anthropic and other players in the AI space, enter into licensing agreements with Reddit, the opportunity could increase further.
Regardless of the final negotiated amounts, I believe these deals could become substantially more valuable because data is becoming increasingly important as human-written content becomes more scarce. As a result, Reddit may be able to charge more for access to its data and establish a more premium position in the market.
Reddit's management team appears to recognize this opportunity and has taken active steps to restrict public access to its data. For example, as of the time of writing, Reddit has announced changes involving RSS feeds, public API access, and access to Old Reddit. The planned restrictions include the removal of RSS feeds on November 13, 2026, restrictions on public API access by March 2027, and limits on Old Reddit access for newer users.
The days of Reddit freely distributing its data are becoming less common. I find it difficult to believe that major AI companies will simply walk away from one of the largest sources of human-written content in the world. Companies such as Anthropic, which have been able to scrape publicly available content, may face greater restrictions on access and could eventually have to pay a premium for licensed data.
My thesis is simple: Will major AI players and their large language models (LLMs) ignore one of the world's largest sources of human-written content? Will these models forgo billions of comments, posts, and other forms of human-generated content that could be valuable for training, reference, recommendations, and advertising-related applications?
I highly doubt it.
I believe this information is extremely valuable to advertisers and AI companies alike. As Google adapts to the AI landscape and newer frontier companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic seek to scale their businesses and potentially go public, I think it is only a matter of time before they begin paying two, three, five, or potentially even ten times what they pay Reddit today for AI licensing, assuming they are currently paying for comparable access.
While I do not have the exact metrics to quantify this, I also believe Reddit's AI licensing revenue could carry higher margins than its core advertising business. Selling access to data does not appear to require nearly the same level of capital investment or employee resources as operating and continually improving a large-scale advertising business. If licensing revenue grows substantially without requiring a proportional increase in operating expenses, it could contribute disproportionately to Reddit's profitability and free cash flow.
Company Valuation
According to analyst consensus estimates, Reddit is projected to generate earnings per share (EPS) of $5.39 in 2026, $7.11 in 2027, and $8.93 in 2028. Based on a share price of approximately $138, these estimates imply forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios of roughly 25.6 for 2026, 19.4 for 2027, and 15.5 for 2028.
However, Reddit has a tendency to beat earnings expectations by substantial margins. I believe analysts may be underestimating the company's future earnings potential.
For example, analysts are projecting approximately 31% EPS growth in 2027. Yet, in Q2 2026 alone, Reddit grew EPS by 177% year over year, while EPS over the last 12 months is up approximately 290%. Given these results, I believe a projected 30% earnings growth rate for 2027 could be materially understating Reddit's potential.
In my personal model, I believe Reddit could generate more than $10 in EPS in 2028, rather than the consensus estimate of $8.93. Even using the current consensus estimates, however, I believe Reddit looks inexpensive relative to its growth and profitability.
At a share price of approximately $138, Reddit has a market capitalization of around $26.5 billion. The company has generated almost exactly $1 billion in free cash flow over the last 12 months. At those levels, its price-to-free-cash-flow ratio is approximately 26.5.
That multiple is not dramatically above the broader market's average. However, Reddit is not growing at an average rate. Its free cash flow increased 135% year over year in the most recent quarter and approximately 156% over the last 12 months. In my view, a company growing its cash generation at these rates deserves to be evaluated differently from a typical business.
Based on Reddit's user trends, rising revenue per user, improving monetization, and potential AI licensing deals, I believe it is very possible that the company could generate more than $2 billion in annual free cash flow within the next year or so.
Consider what that would mean at the current market capitalization of $26.5 billion. If Reddit generated $2 billion in annual free cash flow, its price-to-free-cash-flow ratio would fall to approximately 13.3.
In my opinion, a multiple of around 13 times free cash flow would be exceptionally low for a company growing its revenue and profitability significantly faster than the average company in the market.
I believe that, based strictly on free cash flow, Reddit could generate so much cash over the next one to two years that maintaining a share price around $138 would become difficult to justify financially, assuming the company executes on its growth opportunities.
Furthermore, that scenario assumes only $2 billion in annual free cash flow within the next year or two. Looking three to five years out, I believe Reddit could potentially generate $3 billion, $4 billion, or even $5 billion in annual free cash flow, depending on execution and the ultimate value of its AI licensing agreements.
The moral of the story: Reddit has premium growth, premium profitability, and premium margins, but in my opinion, it trades at a below-average to average-at-best valuation.
Risks
Risk #1: Rapid Changes in AI, Distribution, and Communication
In an ever-changing world of AI, the ways people distribute, communicate, and consume content are constantly evolving. Reddit could end up on the negative side of these changes if communication and distribution channels change rapidly.
Risk #2: Stagnating Monetization Improvements
While I believe this is the lower risk, Reddit's monetization improvements could stagnate or lag behind those of its peers. If Reddit fails to capitalize on its massive amount of data and written content, or if it cannot translate that content into considerable advertising conversions, its revenue per user could slow or stagnate.
Risk #3: Legal and Regulatory Risk
Although Reddit operates as a walled garden, regulatory changes could limit its ability to collect and track data for its models, potentially hurting its monetization rates.
Additionally, lawsuits from companies such as Anthropic could result in unfavorable outcomes for Reddit, potentially affecting its AI licensing deals with Anthropic as well as its agreements with other major partners, including Google and OpenAI.
Risk #4: Synthetic Data and AI-Generated Content
In my opinion, one of Reddit's biggest risks is that synthetic data, meaning AI-generated content, could overtake the platform and undermine the originality of Reddit's content.
Reddit's platform is seen as human, authentic, and genuine. If AI bots take over the platform, they could damage the user experience and undermine one of Reddit's core differentiators. This could create significant downside risk for the business.
Conclusion & Price Targets Conclusion
Reddit is a unique and compelling platform that I believe is a second-order beneficiary of the AI wave. Its business model and financials are attractive for long-term shareholders, and its valuation is heavily skewed in shareholders' favor, assuming the company executes on its opportunities.
I believe the risks are relatively low compared with the potential upside and the predictability of Reddit's future growth.
In conclusion, I am long Reddit and consider it a compelling investment opportunity. I view Reddit as a strong buy for 2026.

I believe this is a more than reasonable valuation for a company growing at Reddit's rate, with its margins, fundamentals, and additional upside opportunities.
Bull Case: $300 per Share
If AI licensing deals and revenue come in above analyst expectations, and user and EPS growth do not slow nearly as much as analysts currently estimate, Reddit could have significant upside.
Instead of generating the consensus estimate of $7.11 in EPS in 2027, Reddit could potentially generate a much higher figure, such as $7.58 or $8.50. Under that scenario, I believe the company could easily see a rerating to $300 or more per share.
That may seem far-fetched at the moment, but I would not be surprised if Reddit's results come in above expectations.
2030 Price Target: $500 per Share
My final price target is $500 per share by 2030.
At $500 per share, Reddit would have a market capitalization of approximately $100 billion, or slightly less, based on today's shares outstanding.
I believe Reddit could be generating somewhere between $4 billion and $6 billion in annual free cash flow by 2030, assuming current trends remain relatively consistent. Even if growth rates regress over time, I believe generating $4 billion to $6 billion in annual free cash flow is absolutely possible.

Annual EPS growth Year-five EPS Implied share price Annualized price return 10% $33.43 $1,170 2.4% 12% $36.59 $1,281 4.3% 15% $41.76 $1,461 7.1%

My tentative conclusion: strong operating performance alone doesn’t settle the valuation question; the eventual multiple materially changes the outcome.

text:
I love Anthropic's products, BUT I think their S1 is a far more scarier than people let on.

Before I get into my analysis, let me just say that I use Claude every day and really like Anthropic's products. But I think they are making a pretty large error with their IPO, trying to slide some things by without you noticing.
When you only look at the top 25 pages of the S-1, everything pretty much looks pretty good: Revenues up from $1.16B in H1 2025 to $16.3B in H1 2026. Q2 2026 GAAP operating profit was $1.03B. They have $131.7B in cash and near-cash equivalents. But if you look at the accounting mechanics, the accounting treatments, the working capital loops, and particularly footnote 9, you start to see that the structure of Anthropic is poised to be that of a high margin software company, while the balance sheet looks more like a highly leveraged utility. This is 100% GAAP-compliant, audited accounting and not considered illegal.
Here are some red flags I found:
Training costs are number uno, there is no gross margin line item anywhere in the S-1. If you open virtually any SaaS S-1 you will see the revenue line, and directly below that COGs or Gross Profit line, then operating expenses. Anthropic has chosen to remove the gross margin line. They have taken their cost of goods sold (customer inference & computing power) and model training cost and put them into a single line aggregate expense called "Compute and infrastructure," which came to $8.95B in H1 2026.
They only have two reasons for doing so:
One either the company has absolutely dreadful marginal profitability per unit provided (not too profitable at the service level) or the multi-billion dollar training campaigns that go on nearly all the time (AI Labs are continuously training the next model; model development doesn't stop) are essential recurring capex rather than optional discretionary R&D spend.
Convertible Notes Subsidy:
So take a look at the bottom of the income statement. There's a large amount of losses in Q2 2026 for changes in the fair value of the convertible notes amounting to $72.4B. Most of the wall street crowd will just brush it off as a non-cash accounting item, as the valuation of notes had gone up by a considerable amount in their last private funding rounds. But if you take a deeper look at those tens of billions of dollars of losses in the form of convertible notes issued by the company between 2023 and 2025 were entirely and soley to cover the enormous training compute costs, which were paid for by the company in the form of cheap equity shares to Google and Amazon (the cloud providers). So I hypothesize that Anthropic is subsidizing their training expense, as part of notes to the Cloud providers Google and Amazon, to shift the Billions of dolllars from top line COGs, into liabilities and R&D. This is 100% GAAP-compliant, audited accounting; it is not illegal, or considered fraud. I'll cover the next part in a second.
Off-Balance Sheet Tsunami:
The $587 billion take-or-pay obligation trap (Footnote 9 of S-1): Total off balance sheet liabilites were up to nearly 6x what they were a year earlier, reaching $587B by the end of Q2 2026
Lets break the numbers down a bit to see where we are:
$265.6B in irrevocable minimum fixed purchase agreements (which includes at least $114.5B to Google Cloud through 2033 and $110B to AWS through 2036); around 80% of that is non-discretionary.
Uncommeced leases, under ASC 842 the leases can be deferred indefinitely until the date of official occupancy, so this category of leases alone make up about $321.4B of off balance sheet liabilites, even though they represent a real liability to the company.
Broadcom 9% debt loop, of that, it contains $161.2B of Broadcom TPU leases which are 5 years out (around 2030,2031) that were funded with $42B 9% loan facility
So how does this like affect the S-1:
Whenever the company uses those loans to make lease payments they are treated as financing activities rather than operating expenses which allows the company to present the cash-flow are relatively clean, presenting the image that Anthropic is profitable or has decent margins. Typically, if you are leasing out infrastructure, it would be a variable cost as most companies do that scales as usage scales, but in Anthropics case they have effectively turned a variable cost into a fixed cost floor that is irrevocable. They have locked themselves into an exponential growth plan without room for any hitches. They are now forced to produce a spike in revenue before 2027-2030 to service the uncommenced leases, take-or-pay commitments, and regular operations.
So now we see the company is using liabilities as a way to shift expenses but they are doing something weird with revenue too:
Notice the weirdness of the balance sheet: revenues go up steadily, so do their current liabilities, seemingly in lockstep. After I traced the path of the funds, you realize that they are creating a self-looping cycle involving Google/AWS: 48%. of the revenue came through the AWS marketplaces and Google Vertex AI Platform (up from 11% in 2023). Gross vs Net revenue inflation: when a customer pays Anthropic for service via the AWS or Google cloud marketplaces, they are recognizing the full amount as gross revenue (which inflates their sales multiples). The commission paid to the marketplace owner (around 20-27%) is then essentially shifted into the sales and marketing expense line at 19% of all revenue.
Working capital vice effect: 58% of the company's accounts receivable are still in the hands of AWS/Google. The other side of it is that current liabilities and accruals have risen so dramatically that they owe a massive amount to their marketplace owners. They are borrowing picks and shovels to mine for gold at Amazon/Google, sell the gold back to them via the marketplaces, have Amazone/Google hold on to 58% of the receivables from the customers, and book the 255 net margin from the marketplaces as gross revenue.
My Conclusion:
The point I am trying to convey is the fact that Private investors and hyperscalers have reached maximum asset concentrations. They have entered massive commitments with cloud providers in order to fuel hypergrowth necessary for inflating valuations. And now those same agreements are chaining them to a death-trap treadmill without an exit strategy. Even with unstable public markets and enterprise cutbacks looming, this offering seems more like a desperate liquidity release than a fundraising exercise. And if revenue growth breaks the form needed to service Anthropic's or any large AI startup's liabilities, the broader market is in trouble.
Edit: Tightened up my phrasing around the Convertible Notes section; I am in no way saying Anthropic is doing something illegal or breaking GAAP compliance; I am just highlighting the choices around their accounting practices. And to clarify the mechanics, I understand that compute invoices still hit the compute and infrastructure OpEx and the $72.4B charge is an unrealized equity fair-value mark on notes; my point is that the economic round trip of issuing cheap convertible debt to cloud providers to fund the cash needed for the massive compute bills is a massive hidden cost of capital

text:
The AI capex boom is increasingly a bet on AGI, not current economics

I think analysts are missing something big by considering AI frontier labs as though they were normal companies making big investments and expecting realistic business outcomes. I want to posit that the AI bubble differs from earlier bubbles because the spending is being justified by quasi-religious beliefs about what AI might eventually become. After reading Adam Becker's More Everything Forever, I’ve started to see the frontier AI race as a billionaire-funded cargo cult: the belief that if enough GPUs, power, data centers, researchers, and capital are accumulated, something qualitatively new will emerge, an AGI or superintelligence that equates to a machine god.
It's basically a science-fiction investment thesis. It sounds crazy, but there's a literal network of rationalist, effective-altruist, and existential-risk thinkers who've spent years treating AGI as a civilization-altering event long before ChatGPT arrived, and those ideas have shaped many of the companies, investors, and researchers now driving the industry. You can verify this. If AGI is truly only a few years away, almost any level of spending can seem rational: frontier labs do not need sustainable business models today because losing billions is preferable to slowing down and letting a competitor reach the prize first.
AI is not fake or useless. LLMs can write code, summarize documents, automate office work, and support research, even if the economics are shaky on some of it. The problem is the belief that models will turn into superintelligent 'beings' if we just pour enough resources into them. I suspect some big players know this: NVIDIA is happy to profit by selling the infrastructure even if Jensen knows its bullshit, Microsoft through Mustafa Suleyman has basically called BS on a lot of this, Google falls somewhere in the middle, and Meta is trying to turn it into a useful consumer product (which I also don't think will work, but that's another issue). In the end, most customers will care less about AGI than whether AI saves enough money to justify the bill.
The bubble bursting will still hurt these companies, but in the end I think may come out okay in the end, but there may be pain along the way. OpenAI and Anthropic are a lot shakier, and I'm curious to see how long they can drag this out: it could be a while. Look how long Elon has been pumping pipe dreams that never happen.
